assumptions.condition: The observed vertices \(A,Y\) have the bow ADMG \(A\to Y\) and \(A\leftrightarrow Y\), represented by a nonparametric latent-variable SCM.

standard.name: Nonparametric SCM Markov to a bow ADMG

assumptions.condition: The realized outcome satisfies \(Y=Y(A)\) almost surely.
Every candidate bow SCM satisfies \(\mathcal L(Y(a)\mid A=a)\sim\mathcal L(Y(a))\).

standard.name: Mutual absolute continuity of observational and interventional arm laws

assumptions.condition: The observations \((A_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n\) are independent and identically distributed draws from the observed bow-SCM law.

One global nonparametric latent-variable SCM has observed vertices \(X,A,Y\), observed arrows \(X\to A\), \(X\to Y\), and \(A\to Y\), and a latent variable \(U\) that may be a parent of each of \(X,A,Y\).

There is a constant \(0<\kappa\le1/2\) and a measurable propensity system \(\boldsymbol e=(e_0,e_1)\) on \(\mathcal X\) such that \(e_a(x)\in[\kappa,1-\kappa]\) and \(e_0(x)+e_1(x)=1\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
The global SCM satisfies \(Y=Y(A)\) almost surely.
For both arms on one common measurable \(\mu_X\)-conull set, the conditional interventional kernel is absolutely continuous with respect to the observed arm kernel: \(Q_a(x,\cdot)\ll P_a(x,\cdot)\).

definitions.name: \(\mathfrak M_e(P)\)
definitions.construction: For \(0<e<1\), \(\mathfrak M_e(P)=\{Q\in\mathcal P(\mathcal Y): Q=\mathcal L(Y(a))\text{ in a bow-ADMG SCM with }\Pr(A=a)=e,\ \mathcal L(Y\mid A=a)=P,\text{ and member properties }\mathrm{ass:bow\text{-}structure},\mathrm{ass:consistency},\mathrm{ass:positivity},\mathrm{ass:mutual\text{-}ac}\}\). At the boundary, define \(\mathfrak M_1(P)=\{P\}\).

definitions.name: \(\mathfrak L_e(P)\)
definitions.construction: For \(0<e\le1\), \(\mathfrak L_e(P)=\{Q\in\mathcal P(\mathcal Y): Q=eP+(1-e)R\text{ for some }R\in\mathcal P(\mathcal Y)\text{ with }R\ll P\}\); hence \(\mathfrak L_1(P)=\{P\}\).

definitions.name: \(\mathfrak H_c\)
definitions.construction: \(\{f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R: f\text{ is finite, continuous, convex, }f(1)=0,\text{ and there exists }b\in\mathbb R\text{ such that }g_b(t)=f(t)-b(t-1)\text{ obeys }g_b(t)=0\text{ for }0\le t\le c\text{ and }g_b(t)>0\text{ for }t>c\}\).

definitions.name: \(L_e,U_e\)
definitions.construction: For \(0\le e\le1\), \(L_e(p)=e p\) for \(0\le p<1\), \(L_e(1)=1\), \(U_e(0)=0\), and \(U_e(p)=e p+1-e\) for \(0<p\le1\). In particular, \(L_1(p)=U_1(p)=p\) for every \(p\in[0,1]\).

definitions.name: \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_{n,\alpha}\)
definitions.construction: Let \(n_a=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}\), \(\delta_e=\sqrt{\log(4/\alpha)/(2n)}\), and \(\delta_F=\sqrt{\log(4/\alpha)/(2n_a)}\) when \(n_a>0\). Form \(I_e=[\widehat e_n-\delta_e,\widehat e_n+\delta_e]\cap[0,1]\) and \(I_F(y)=[\widehat F_{P,n}(y)-\delta_F,\widehat F_{P,n}(y)+\delta_F]\cap[0,1]\). For every \(y\), \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_{n,\alpha}(y)\) is the coordinatewise rectangular hull of \(\{(L_\eta(p),U_\eta(p)):\eta\in I_e,\ p\in I_F(y)\}\); when \(n_a=0\), set it to \([0,1]^2\).

definitions.name: \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{dir}}\)
definitions.construction: Handle: linearize the joint pre-endpoint empirical process \((\widehat e_n,\widehat F_{P,n})\), derive the Hadamard directional derivative of the piecewise map \((e,F_P)\mapsto(L_e\circ F_P,U_e\circ F_P)\), and estimate that derivative inside a Fang--Santos multiplier or numerical-delta bootstrap before taking the supremum over thresholds and arms.

definitions.name: \(\mathfrak M^{\to}_e(P)\)
definitions.construction: For \(0<e<1\), \(\mathfrak M^{\to}_e(P)\) is the set of laws \(Q=\mathcal L(Y(a))\) realized in a nonparametric latent-variable bow-ADMG SCM with \(\Pr(A=a)=e\), \(\mathcal L(Y\mid A=a)=P\), and member properties \(\mathrm{ass:bow\text{-}structure}\), \(\mathrm{ass:consistency}\), and \(\mathrm{ass:positivity}\), without imposing \(\mathrm{ass:mutual\text{-}ac}\). At the boundary define \(\mathfrak M^{\to}_1(P)=\{P\}\).

definitions.name: \(\mathfrak L^{\to}_e(P)\)
definitions.construction: For \(0<e\le1\), \(\mathfrak L^{\to}_e(P)=\{Q\in\mathcal P(\mathcal Y):Q=eP+(1-e)R\text{ for some }R\in\mathcal P(\mathcal Y)\}\); hence \(\mathfrak L^{\to}_1(P)=\{P\}\).

definitions.name: \(L^{\to}_e,U^{\to}_e\)
definitions.construction: For \(0\le e\le1\) and \(0\le p\le1\), define \(L^{\to}_e(p)=ep\) and \(U^{\to}_e(p)=ep+1-e\).

definitions.name: \(\mathfrak M^{\to}_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\)
definitions.construction: Let \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\) be standard Borel spaces, let \(\mu_X\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\), let \(0<\kappa\le1/2\), let \(\boldsymbol e=(e_0,e_1)\) satisfy \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}overlap}\), and let \(\boldsymbol P=(P_0,P_1)\) be Markov kernels from \(\mathcal X\) to \(\mathcal Y\).  Then \(\mathfrak M^{\to}_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\) is the set of pairs \(\boldsymbol Q=(Q_0,Q_1)\) of Markov kernels for which one SCM satisfying \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}bow\text{-}architecture}\), \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}overlap}\), and \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}consistency}\) has \(X\sim\mu_X\) and admits one measurable \(\mu_X\)-conull set \(S\) on which, simultaneously for \(a=0,1\), \(\Pr(A=a\mid X=x)=e_a(x)\), \(\mathcal L(Y\mid A=a,X=x)=P_a(x,\cdot)\), and \(\mathcal L(Y(a)\mid X=x)=Q_a(x,\cdot)\).  Conditional kernels are versions and no restriction is placed on \(S^c\).  No reverse-support condition is imposed.

definitions.name: \(\mathfrak L^{\to}_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\)
definitions.construction:
Under the same self-contained setup of standard Borel \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\), \(\mu_X\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\), \(0<\kappa\le1/2\), measurable \(\boldsymbol e=(e_0,e_1)\) satisfying \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}overlap}\), and Markov kernels \(\boldsymbol P=(P_0,P_1)\), the class \(\mathfrak L^{\to}_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\) consists of pairs \(\boldsymbol Q=(Q_0,Q_1)\) of Markov kernels for which there are Markov kernels \(\boldsymbol R=(R_0,R_1)\) and one measurable \(\mu_X\)-conull set \(S\) such that, for every \(x\in S\) and \(a=0,1\),
\[
 Q_a(x,\cdot)=e_a(x)P_a(x,\cdot)+(1-e_a(x))R_a(x,\cdot).
\]
No restriction is imposed on the versions over \(S^c\).

definitions.name: \(\mathfrak M_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\)
definitions.construction: Let \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\) be standard Borel spaces, let \(\mu_X\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\), let \(0<\kappa\le1/2\), let measurable \(\boldsymbol e=(e_0,e_1)\) satisfy \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}overlap}\), and let \(\boldsymbol P=(P_0,P_1)\) be Markov kernels from \(\mathcal X\) to \(\mathcal Y\).  Then \(\mathfrak M_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\) is the set of pairs \(\boldsymbol Q=(Q_0,Q_1)\) for which one SCM satisfying \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}bow\text{-}architecture}\), \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}overlap}\), and \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}consistency}\) has \(X\sim\mu_X\) and admits one measurable \(\mu_X\)-conull set \(S\) on which, simultaneously for \(a=0,1\), \(\Pr(A=a\mid X=x)=e_a(x)\), \(\mathcal L(Y\mid A=a,X=x)=P_a(x,\cdot)\), \(\mathcal L(Y(a)\mid X=x)=Q_a(x,\cdot)\), and \(Q_a(x,\cdot)\ll P_a(x,\cdot)\).  Conditional kernels are versions and no restriction is placed on \(S^c\).

definitions.name: \(\mathfrak L_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\)
definitions.construction: Under the same self-contained setup of standard Borel \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\), \(\mu_X\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\), \(0<\kappa\le1/2\), measurable \(\boldsymbol e=(e_0,e_1)\) satisfying \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}overlap}\), and Markov kernels \(\boldsymbol P=(P_0,P_1)\), the class \(\mathfrak L_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\) consists of pairs \(\boldsymbol Q=(Q_0,Q_1)\) for which there are Markov kernels \(\boldsymbol R=(R_0,R_1)\) and one measurable \(\mu_X\)-conull set \(S\) such that \(Q_a=e_aP_a+(1-e_a)R_a\) and \(R_a(x,\cdot)\ll P_a(x,\cdot)\) for both arms and every \(x\in S\).  No restriction is imposed on the versions over \(S^c\).

definitions.name: \(\mathfrak B^{\mathrm{ad},\to}_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\)
definitions.construction:
Let \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\) be standard Borel spaces, let \(\mu_X\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\), let \(0<\kappa\le1/2\), let measurable \(\boldsymbol e=(e_0,e_1)\) satisfy \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}overlap}\), and let \(\boldsymbol P=(P_0,P_1)\) be Markov kernels from \(\mathcal X\) to \(\mathcal Y\).  Define \(f_{a,x}(t)=(t-1/e_a(x))_+\).  The class \(\mathfrak B^{\mathrm{ad},\to}_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\) consists of pairs \(\boldsymbol Q=(Q_0,Q_1)\) of Markov kernels from \(\mathcal X\) to \(\mathcal Y\) for which there is one measurable \(\mu_X\)-conull set \(S\) such that, for every \(x\in S\) and \(a=0,1\), \(P_a(x,\cdot)\ll Q_a(x,\cdot)\) and
\[
 D_{f_{a,x}}(P_a(x,\cdot)\|Q_a(x,\cdot))\le B_{f_{a,x}}(e_a(x)).
\]
The constraints are fiberwise, not integrated over \(x\), and no assertion is made at a specified point in \(S^c\).

definitions.name: \(\mathfrak B^{\mathrm{ad}}_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\)
definitions.construction:
Let \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\) be standard Borel spaces, let \(\mu_X\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\), let \(0<\kappa\le1/2\), let measurable \(\boldsymbol e=(e_0,e_1)\) satisfy \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\text{-}overlap}\), and let \(\boldsymbol P=(P_0,P_1)\) be Markov kernels from \(\mathcal X\) to \(\mathcal Y\).  With \(f_{a,x}(t)=(t-1/e_a(x))_+\), the class \(\mathfrak B^{\mathrm{ad}}_{\mu_X,\boldsymbol e}(\boldsymbol P)\) consists of pairs \(\boldsymbol Q=(Q_0,Q_1)\) of Markov kernels from \(\mathcal X\) to \(\mathcal Y\) for which there is one measurable \(\mu_X\)-conull set \(S\) such that, for every \(x\in S\) and \(a=0,1\), \(P_a(x,\cdot)\sim Q_a(x,\cdot)\) and
\[
 D_{f_{a,x}}(P_a(x,\cdot)\|Q_a(x,\cdot))\le B_{f_{a,x}}(e_a(x)).
\]
The constraints are fiberwise, not integrated over \(x\), and no assertion is made at a specified point in \(S^c\).

statements.statement: For every standard Borel \(\mathcal Y\), arm \(a\), probability law \(P\), and \(0<e<1\), the bow-ADMG compatible interventional laws are exactly the propensity mixtures: \(\mathfrak M_e(P)=\mathfrak L_e(P)\). Equivalently, \(Q\in\mathfrak M_e(P)\) if and only if \(Q=eP+(1-e)R\) for some \(R\ll P\), or if and only if \(Q\sim P\) and \(dP/dQ\le1/e\) \(Q\)-almost surely. Every admissible \(R\) is realized by a latent construction with \(U=(A,Y(0),Y(1))\).
statements.proof_tex:
Fix the objects in the theorem.  If \(Q\in\mathfrak M_e(P)\), consistency and the observed-arm restriction give
\[
 \mathcal L(Y(a)\mid A=a)=\mathcal L(Y\mid A=a)=P.
\]
Because \(0<e<1\), the conditional law
\[
 R=\mathcal L(Y(a)\mid A\ne a)
\]
is a probability law.  For every measurable \(B\subseteq\mathcal Y\), the law of total probability gives
\[
 Q(B)=\Pr\{Y(a)\in B\}=eP(B)+(1-e)R(B). \tag{1}
\]
The mutual-absolute-continuity member property says \(P\sim Q\), in particular \(Q\ll P\).  If \(P(B)=0\), then \(Q(B)=0\), and (1), nonnegativity, and \(1-e>0\) imply \(R(B)=0\).  Hence \(R\ll P\), proving \(\mathfrak M_e(P)\subseteq\mathfrak L_e(P)\).

Conversely, suppose
\[
 Q=eP+(1-e)R,\qquad R\ll P. \tag{2}
\]
On a standard Borel probability space, draw \(A\) with \(\Pr(A=a)=e\); conditionally on \(A=a\), draw \(Y(a)\) with law \(P\), and conditionally on \(A\ne a\), draw \(Y(a)\) with law \(R\).  Draw \(Y(1-a)\), conditionally independently given \(A\), from any fixed probability law, for example \(P\).  Put \(U=(A,Y(0),Y(1))\), let the treatment structural equation return the \(A\)-coordinate of \(U\), and let the outcome structural equation return \(Y(A)\).  These measurable structural equations form a nonparametric latent-variable SCM Markov to the bow ADMG: the common latent input permits \(A\leftrightarrow Y\), and the selector equation uses the arrow \(A\to Y\).  The construction satisfies consistency, has propensity \(e\), and has observed arm law \(P\).  Equation (2) is exactly its law of \(Y(a)\).

Moreover, (2) implies \(Q\ge eP\), so \(P\ll Q\), while \(R\ll P\) implies \(Q\ll P\).  Thus \(P\sim Q\), and the constructed SCM satisfies the mutual-absolute-continuity member property.  This proves \(\mathfrak L_e(P)\subseteq\mathfrak M_e(P)\), hence equality.

It remains to prove the likelihood-ratio characterization.  Under (2), let \(r=dP/dQ\), which exists because \(P\ll Q\).  The measure inequality \(Q-eP\ge0\) is equivalent to
\[
 1-er\ge0\qquad Q\text{-almost surely},
\]
and therefore \(r\le1/e\), \(Q\)-almost surely.  We already proved \(Q\ll P\), so \(Q\sim P\).  Conversely, suppose \(Q\sim P\) and \(r=dP/dQ\le1/e\), \(Q\)-almost surely.  Define
\[
 R(B)=\frac{Q(B)-eP(B)}{1-e}
     =\int_B\frac{1-er}{1-e}\,dQ.
\]
The displayed density is nonnegative, and its integral is
\[
 \frac{1-e\int r\,dQ}{1-e}=1,
\]
so \(R\) is a probability law and (2) holds.  Since \(Q\ll P\), every \(P\)-null set is also \(Q\)-null and hence \(R\)-null, so \(R\ll P\).  The preceding construction realizes this \(R\), completing every asserted equivalence and the realization claim.
statements.justification: This theorem is the abstract fixed-fiber structural input; the new conditional theorem proves measurable simultaneous realization rather than evaluating this result at a version-dependent covariate point.
statements.gap: Jung and Kang prove outer validity but do not prove realization of every fixed-fiber mixture by the bow SCM.
statements.consumer: It supports the fixed-propensity generator frontier and fixed-stratum CDF and inference consequences.

statements.statement: Fix \(0<e<1\) and \(c=1/e\). For every finite continuous convex \(f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) with \(f(1)=0\), the following are equivalent: \(\mathfrak B_{f,e}(P)=\mathfrak L_e(P)\) for every probability law \(P\) on every standard Borel space; this equality holds for every full-support binary \(P\); and \(f\in\mathfrak H_c\). Thus, modulo the divergence-invariant affine term \(b(t-1)\), exactness holds if and only if the generator vanishes on \([0,1/e]\) and is strictly positive on \((1/e,\infty)\).
statements.proof_tex:
Fix \(0<e<1\) and put \(c=1/e\).  If \(P\ll Q\) and \(r=dP/dQ\), then \(\int r\,dQ=1\).  Consequently, for every \(b\in\mathbb R\), replacing \(f\) by
\[
 f_b(t)=f(t)-b(t-1)
\]
changes neither the divergence nor the calibrated radius, because
\[
 \int(r-1)\,dQ=0,
 \qquad
 e(c-1)+(1-e)(0-1)=0. \tag{2}
\]
Convexity gives the chord inequality
\[
 f(t)\le \left(1-\frac{t}{c}\right)f(0)+\frac{t}{c}f(c),
 \qquad 0\le t\le c. \tag{3}
\]

If \(Q\in\mathfrak L_e(P)\), the mixture characterization in \(\mathrm{thm:bow\text{-}mixture\text{-}completeness}\) gives \(Q\sim P\) and \(r\le c\), \(Q\)-almost surely.  Integrating (3), using \(\int r\,dQ=1\) and \(1/c=e\), yields
\[
 D_f(P\|Q)
 \le \left(1-\frac1c\right)f(0)+\frac1c f(c)
 =(1-e)f(0)+ef(c)=B_f(e). \tag{4}
\]
Thus \(\mathfrak L_e(P)\subseteq\mathfrak B_{f,e}(P)\) for every admissible generator.

Suppose first that \(f\in\mathfrak H_c\).  By definition there is \(b\) such that \(g(t)=f(t)-b(t-1)\) vanishes on \([0,c]\) and is strictly positive on \((c,\infty)\).  In particular \(g\ge0\), and
\[
 B_g(e)=eg(c)+(1-e)g(0)=0. \tag{5}
\]
For \(Q\in\mathfrak B_{f,e}(P)\), mutual support supplies \(r=dP/dQ\), and affine invariance (2) gives
\[
 0\le \int g(r)\,dQ=D_g(P\|Q)=D_f(P\|Q)\le B_f(e)=B_g(e)=0.
\]
Hence \(g(r)=0\), \(Q\)-almost surely, and strict positivity above \(c\) implies \(r\le c\), \(Q\)-almost surely.  The likelihood-ratio characterization in the preceding theorem now gives \(Q\in\mathfrak L_e(P)\).  Together with (4), this proves universal exactness.

For necessity, assume equality for every full-support binary \(P\).  Write \(P=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\), \(p\in(0,1)\), and \(Q_q=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)\).  The law \(Q_{ep}\) is the mixture of \(P\) and \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0)\), and the residual is absolutely continuous with respect to full-support \(P\); hence \(Q_{ep}\in\mathfrak L_e(P)\).  For \(0<q<ep\), the likelihood ratio on the success cell is \(p/q>c\), so \(Q_q\notin\mathfrak L_e(P)\).  Exactness therefore gives
\[
 D_f(P\|Q_{ep})\le B_f(e),
 \qquad
 D_f(P\|Q_q)>B_f(e)\quad(0<q<ep). \tag{6}
\]
The binary divergence
\[
 q\longmapsto qf(p/q)+(1-q)f((1-p)/(1-q))
\]
is continuous on \((0,1)\).  Letting \(q\uparrow ep\) in (6) proves the boundary equality
\[
 epf(c)+(1-ep)f\!\left(\frac{1-p}{1-ep}\right)=B_f(e). \tag{7}
\]
Letting \(p\downarrow0\) in (7), using finiteness and continuity of \(f\) and \(f(1)=0\), gives
\[
 B_f(e)=0. \tag{8}
\]

Normalize by setting \(g(t)=f(t)+f(0)(t-1)\).  By affine invariance, \(B_g(e)=0\), while
\[
 g(0)=g(1)=0,
 \qquad
 0=B_g(e)=eg(c)+(1-e)g(0)
\]
implies \(g(c)=0\).  Applying (7) to \(g\) yields
\[
 g\!\left(\frac{1-p}{1-ep}\right)=0,\qquad 0<p<1. \tag{9}
\]
The argument of \(g\) in (9) ranges over \((0,1)\); continuity therefore gives \(g=0\) on \([0,1]\).

Let \(y\in(1,c)\), choose \(x\in(0,1)\), and put \(\lambda=(1-x)/(y-x)\).  Give one cell \(Q\)-mass \(\lambda\), the other mass \(1-\lambda\), and obtain \(P\) by multiplying these masses by \(y\) and \(x\), respectively.  Because
\[
 \lambda y+(1-\lambda)x=1,
\]
these are full-support probability laws, and both likelihood ratios are at most \(c\).  Hence \(Q\in\mathfrak L_e(P)\), and exactness, convexity at the mean-one likelihood ratio, and (8) give
\[
 0=g(1)\le D_g(P\|Q)
   =\lambda g(y)+(1-\lambda)g(x)\le B_g(e)=0.
\]
Since \(g(x)=0\) and \(\lambda>0\), it follows that \(g(y)=0\).  Thus \(g=0\) on \([0,c]\).

For \(t>c\), express \(c\) as a strict convex combination of \(1\) and \(t\).  Convexity and \(g(1)=g(c)=0\) imply \(g(t)\ge0\).  If \(g(t)=0\), choose any \(x\in(0,1)\) and repeat the preceding two-ratio construction with ratios \(t\) and \(x\).  It gives full-support binary laws with
\[
 D_g(P\|Q)=0=B_g(e),
\]
so \(Q\in\mathfrak B_{f,e}(P)\), but the ratio \(t>c\) excludes \(Q\) from \(\mathfrak L_e(P)\), contradicting exactness.  Hence \(g(t)>0\) for every \(t>c\), which is exactly \(f\in\mathfrak H_c\).  Universal exactness plainly implies binary exactness, and the bow-mixture theorem identifies the mixture class with the compatible causal class, completing the three-way equivalence.
statements.justification: The affine-invariant iff gives the exact cap-detecting geometry at a fixed propensity and is paired with the conditional adaptive-hinge theorem.
statements.gap: Prior divergence and density-band work does not characterize all ordinary convex generators yielding causal feasible-set equality.
statements.consumer: It explains both the adaptive conditional construction and the impossibility of a single exact generator across distinct propensities.

statements.statement: Fix \(0<e<1\), let \(c=1/e\), and suppose \(f\notin\mathfrak H_c\). There is a nonempty Euclidean-open set \(\mathcal O_f\subset(0,1)^2\) of binary pairs \((p,q)\), interpreted as \(P=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) and \(Q=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)\), such that \(Q\in\mathfrak B_{f,e}(P)\setminus\mathfrak L_e(P)\) throughout \(\mathcal O_f\). More precisely, either no affine representative of \(f\) is affine on \([0,c]\), in which case \(\mathcal O_f\) can be chosen with \(D_f(P\|Q)<B_f(e)\), or an affine representative vanishes on \([0,c]\) and on \([0,d]\) for some \(d>c\), in which case an open illegal set is contained in the zero-divergence face. This dichotomy includes nondifferentiable and piecewise-linear generators.
statements.proof_tex:
Fix \(0<e<1\), put \(c=1/e\), and define the chord of \(f\) between \(0\) and \(c\) by
\[
 \ell(t)=\left(1-\frac tc\right)f(0)+\frac tc f(c).
\]
Convexity gives \(f(t)\le\ell(t)\) on \([0,c]\), and
\[
 \ell(1)=(1-e)f(0)+ef(c)=B_f(e). \tag{6}
\]
Subtracting an affine function does not change whether a function is affine on an interval.  Thus the first case in the statement is precisely the case in which \(f\) is not affine on \([0,c]\).

Assume first that \(f\) is not affine on \([0,c]\).  Then
\[
 f(x)<\ell(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in(0,c). \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, \(h=\ell-f\) is concave and nonnegative on \([0,c]\), with \(h(0)=h(c)=0\).  If \(h(x_0)=0\) at one interior point, concavity applied first with endpoints \(x<x_0<c\) and then with endpoints \(0<x_0<x\) forces \(h(x)=0\) on both sides of \(x_0\), contradicting non-affinity.

Choose \(x\in(0,1)\), let
\[
 \lambda=\frac{1-x}{c-x},\qquad q_0=\lambda,\qquad p_0=c\lambda,
\]
and put \(P_0=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_0)\), \(Q_0=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q_0)\).  Since \(c>1\) and \(0<x<1\), both laws have full support.  Their likelihood ratios are \(c\) and \(x\), and \(q_0=ep_0\), so \(Q_0\in\mathfrak L_e(P_0)\).  Because affine functions commute with expectation and the two ratios have \(Q_0\)-mean one, (6)--(7) give
\[
 D_f(P_0\|Q_0)
 =\lambda f(c)+(1-\lambda)f(x)
 <\lambda\ell(c)+(1-\lambda)\ell(x)
 =\ell(1)=B_f(e). \tag{8}
\]
The binary divergence is continuous on \((0,1)^2\).  Hence one may choose \(q_1<q_0=ep_0\), sufficiently close to \(q_0\), such that
\[
 D_f\!\left(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_0)\middle\|\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q_1)\right)<B_f(e).
\]
Both strict inequalities \(D_f<B_f(e)\) and \(q<ep\) persist on some nonempty Euclidean-open neighborhood \(\mathcal O_f\) of \((p_0,q_1)\) contained in \((0,1)^2\).  Throughout this neighborhood, \(P\sim Q\), the strict divergence inequality places \(Q\) in \(\mathfrak B_{f,e}(P)\), while \(p/q>c\) excludes \(Q\) from \(\mathfrak L_e(P)\).  This proves the first alternative.

Assume next that \(f\) is affine on \([0,c]\).  Since \(f(1)=0\), there is \(b\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
 g(t)=f(t)-b(t-1)=0,\qquad 0\le t\le c. \tag{9}
\]
Convexity and (9) imply \(g(t)\ge0\) for \(t>c\).  Because \(f\notin\mathfrak H_c\), strict positivity fails: there is \(d>c\) with \(g(d)=0\).  Convexity between \(c\) and \(d\), together with nonnegativity, shows that in fact
\[
 g(t)=0,\qquad 0\le t\le d. \tag{10}
\]
Choose \(x\in(0,1)\) and \(y\in(c,d)\), let \(\lambda=(1-x)/(y-x)\), and form full-support binary laws for which \(dP/dQ\) equals \(y\) on a cell of \(Q\)-mass \(\lambda\) and \(x\) on its complement.  In Bernoulli coordinates this means \(q=\lambda\) and \(p=\lambda y\).  Then \(p/q=y>c\), so the pair is SCM-illegal, whereas affine invariance and (10) give
\[
 D_f(P\|Q)=D_g(P\|Q)=0=B_g(e)=B_f(e).
\]
The inequalities \(p/q>c\), \((1-p)/(1-q)\in(0,d)\), and \(p/q<d\) persist on a sufficiently small open neighborhood.  On that neighborhood both likelihood ratios lie in \((0,d)\), so (10) keeps the divergence identically zero, while the cap remains violated.  This is the asserted nonempty open illegal set in the zero-divergence face.  The argument uses only finiteness, continuity, and convexity, and therefore includes kinked and piecewise-linear generators.
statements.justification: Jung--Kang (2026) use Theorem 5 to calibrate the propensity-only divergence radius, define the resulting ambiguity class in equation (10), and optimize causal functionals over it while presenting the framework as sharp partial identification with tight causal bounds. The theorem isolates the exact model distinction: every generator \(f\) outside the hinge class admits a nonempty open set of full-support binary laws accepted by that divergence program but excluded by the bow-SCM feasible set.
statements.gap: Jung--Kang's extrema may be exact for their declared divergence relaxation, but their sharpness presentation does not establish that every law in the ambiguity class is bow-SCM realizable. The open-illegality theorem proves that, for every failing generator, an open set is not realizable, so the corresponding extrema need not be sharp for the bow-SCM model.
statements.consumer: The result gives a robust legality diagnostic for KL, Hellinger, chi-square, total-variation, Jensen--Shannon, and every other failing generator.

statements.statement: Let \(\mathcal Y=\mathbb R\). For every threshold \(y\), write \(p=F_P(y)\). The exact bow-SCM identified interval is \(\{F_Q(y):Q\in\mathfrak M_e(P)\}=[L_e(p),U_e(p)]\). Each endpoint is attained by a bow-ADMG SCM satisfying all maintained support conditions, including when \(P\) has an atom at \(y\), \(p=0\), or \(p=1\). For \(0<p<1\), the witnesses choose residual laws supported on \(({-}\infty,y]\) or its complement; the boundary formulas force the unique value \(0\) or \(1\).
statements.proof_tex:
Fix \(y\in\mathbb R\), put \(B_y=(-\infty,y]\), and write \(p=P(B_y)=F_P(y)\).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:positivity}\) gives \(0<e<1\).  By \(\mathrm{thm:bow\text{-}mixture\text{-}completeness}\), a law \(Q\) belongs to \(\mathfrak M_e(P)\) exactly when
\[
 Q=eP+(1-e)R
 \quad\text{for some probability law }R\ll P.
\]
Consequently, with \(r=R(B_y)\),
\[
 F_Q(y)=Q(B_y)=eP(B_y)+(1-e)R(B_y)=ep+(1-e)r. \tag{1}
\]
Suppose first that \(0<p<1\).  Absolute continuity only implies \(r\in[0,1]\), so (1) gives the inclusion
\[
 \{F_Q(y):Q\in\mathfrak M_e(P)\}\subseteq[ep,ep+1-e]. \tag{2}
\]
For the reverse inclusion, define the conditional probability laws
\[
 P_{B_y}(C)=\frac{P(C\cap B_y)}{p},
 \qquad
 P_{B_y^c}(C)=\frac{P(C\cap B_y^c)}{1-p}
\]
for measurable \(C\subseteq\mathbb R\).  The divisions are valid because \(0<p<1\).  For every \(r\in[0,1]\), let
\[
 R_r=rP_{B_y}+(1-r)P_{B_y^c}.
\]
Both conditional laws, and hence \(R_r\), are absolutely continuous with respect to \(P\), while \(R_r(B_y)=r\).  The completeness theorem therefore supplies a bow-ADMG SCM, with latent variable \(U=(A,Y(0),Y(1))\), realizing
\[
 Q_r=eP+(1-e)R_r
 \quad\text{and}
 \quad F_{Q_r}(y)=ep+(1-e)r.
\]
As \(r\) ranges over \([0,1]\), the last expression ranges over the whole interval in (2).  In particular, \(R_0=P_{B_y^c}\) and \(R_1=P_{B_y}\) attain the lower and upper endpoints and are supported on the complement of \(B_y\) and on \(B_y\), respectively.

If \(p=0\), then \(P(B_y)=0\), so \(R\ll P\) forces \(R(B_y)=0\).  Equation (1) then forces \(F_Q(y)=0\) for every compatible \(Q\).  If \(p=1\), then \(P(B_y^c)=0\), so \(R(B_y^c)=0\), \(R(B_y)=1\), and (1) forces \(F_Q(y)=1\).  In either boundary case \(R=P\) is admissible, so the unique value is attained by the latent bow construction from the completeness theorem.  By \(\mathrm{def:cdf\text{-}maps}\),
\[
 [L_e(p),U_e(p)]
 =
 \begin{cases}
 [0,0],&p=0,\\
 [ep,ep+1-e],&0<p<1,\\
 [1,1],&p=1.
 \end{cases}
\]
This proves the asserted equality and attainment.  The argument depends only on the measurable event \(B_y\), not on whether \(P\) has an atom at \(y\).  It is also exactly the mutual-absolute-continuity branch of \(\mathrm{thm:support\text{-}regime\text{-}cdf\text{-}endpoints\text{-}sharp}\), which distinguishes these boundary values from those obtained when singular residual laws are allowed.
statements.justification: Huber's (1964) unrestricted contamination model yields the event-probability interval \([ep,ep+1-e]\). The delivered contribution is the support split: under mutual absolute continuity the endpoints collapse to the unique values zero and one at \(p=0\) and \(p=1\), respectively, while the formulas remain atom-aware and every endpoint is attained by a bow-ADMG SCM.
statements.gap: Unrestricted Huber contamination supplies the linear interval \([ep,ep+1-e]\), but it does not certify the mutual-absolute-continuity boundary collapse, the atom-aware support cases, or endpoint attainment inside the maintained bow-SCM class.
statements.consumer: It supplies the exact CDF map appropriate to each support convention and the mutual map used for inference.

statements.statement: For every admissible generator \(f\), \(\mathfrak B^{\mathrm{law}}_{f,e}(P)=\mathfrak L_e(P)=\mathfrak M_e(P)\). For each \(h\in L^\infty(P)\), the exact mutual-AC support-function endpoints are \(\underline\theta_h=eE_P[h]+(1-e)\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_P h\) and \(\overline\theta_h=eE_P[h]+(1-e)\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_P h\). On a finite alphabet restricted to \(\operatorname{supp}(P)\), adding the cap constraints \(q_j\ge ep_j\) to a divergence program yields the exact mutual-AC class, weakly tightens every linear bounded-query optimization, and strictly tightens it whenever a unique relaxed optimizer violates the cap. For every \(f\notin\mathfrak H_c\), a bounded binary query has a strict legality gap on a nonempty open region of observational laws.
statements.proof_tex:
Fix \(0<e<1\), put \(c=1/e\), and let \(f\) be any finite continuous convex generator with \(f(1)=0\).  If \(Q\in\mathfrak L_e(P)\), then \(Q=eP+(1-e)R\) for some \(R\ll P\).  Thus \(Q\sim P\), and for \(r=dP/dQ\) one has \(0<r\le c\), \(Q\)-almost surely, and \(\int r\,dQ=1\).  The convex chord inequality on \([0,c]\) yields
\[
 D_f(P\|Q)
 \le\int\left\{\left(1-\frac rc\right)f(0)+\frac rc f(c)\right\}dQ
 =(1-e)f(0)+ef(c)=B_f(e). \tag{11}
\]
Hence \(\mathfrak L_e(P)\subseteq\mathfrak B_{f,e}(P)\).  By the definition of the lawful correction,
\[
 \mathfrak B^{\mathrm{law}}_{f,e}(P)
 =\mathfrak B_{f,e}(P)\cap\mathfrak L_e(P)
 =\mathfrak L_e(P).
\]
The frozen bow-mixture completeness theorem then gives \(\mathfrak L_e(P)=\mathfrak M_e(P)\).

Let \(h\in L^\infty(P)\), and write
\[
 m=\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_P h,\qquad M=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_P h.
\]
For \(Q=eP+(1-e)R\) with \(R\ll P\),
\[
 E_Q[h]=eE_P[h]+(1-e)E_R[h],\qquad m\le E_R[h]\le M. \tag{12}
\]
Thus the claimed expressions bound the infimum and supremum.  Conversely, for every \(\eta>0\), the defining properties of essential infimum and supremum give sets of positive \(P\)-probability
\[
 C^-_\eta=\{h<m+\eta\},\qquad C^+_\eta=\{h>M-\eta\}.
\]
Taking \(R^-_\eta=P(\,\cdot\mid C^-_\eta)\) and \(R^+_\eta=P(\,\cdot\mid C^+_\eta)\), both of which are absolutely continuous with respect to \(P\), and then letting \(\eta\downarrow0\) in (12), proves
\[
 \underline\theta_h=eE_P[h]+(1-e)m,\qquad
 \overline\theta_h=eE_P[h]+(1-e)M. \tag{13}
\]

Now suppose the alphabet is finite and restricted to \(\operatorname{supp}(P)\), so every retained cell has \(p_j>0\).  A probability vector \(q=(q_j)_j\) belongs to \(\mathfrak L_e(P)\) if and only if
\[
 q_j\ge ep_j\quad\text{for every }j. \tag{14}
\]
The forward implication follows from \(q_j=ep_j+(1-e)r_j\).  Conversely, (14) makes
\[
 r_j=\frac{q_j-ep_j}{1-e}
\]
nonnegative with \(\sum_jr_j=1\), and the support restriction gives \(R\ll P\).  By (11), the divergence constraint is redundant on (14).  Therefore adjoining (14) to the divergence program gives exactly the mutual-absolute-continuity compatible class.  Its feasible set is a closed subset of the finite simplex and hence compact.  Restricting a feasible set can only weakly lower a linear maximum and weakly raise a linear minimum.  If a relaxed optimizer is unique and violates (14), equality of the corresponding optimal values would make an optimizer over the compact capped set a second relaxed optimizer, a contradiction.  The tightening is then strict.  The same coordinate argument is consistent with the unrestricted-alphabet formulation in \(\mathrm{thm:one\text{-}sided\text{-}query\text{-}legality\text{-}correction}\).

Finally suppose \(f\notin\mathfrak H_c\).  The construction in \(\mathrm{thm:open\text{-}illegal\text{-}dichotomy}\) yields an open binary set with \(q<ep\) and \(Q\in\mathfrak B_{f,e}(P)\).  It contains a rectangle \(I\times J\) about one of its points.  For every \(p\) in a sufficiently small nonempty open interval \(I\), some \(q\in J\) remains divergence-feasible and satisfies \(q<ep\).  For the bounded success indicator \(h(z)=\mathbf 1\{z=1\}\), the lawful lower endpoint is \(ep\) by (13), whereas the relaxed lower value is at most \(q<ep\).  This is the claimed strict legality gap on an open region of observational laws.
statements.justification: The theorem converts the likelihood-ratio cap into an exact feasible-set intersection and explicit finite-alphabet constraints for generic bounded-query optimization.
statements.gap: The divergence ambiguity class is a valid outer class, but outer-class validity alone does not establish that every feasible law is realizable by the bow SCM; this theorem supplies the generic legality correction without making a claim about a particular procedure.
statements.consumer: Researchers optimizing bounded causal queries on a declared finite alphabet can impose \(q_j\ge ep_j\) to recover the exact bow-SCM feasible set.

statements.statement: Under independent observational sampling, the band \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_{n,\alpha}\) satisfies \(\Pr\{(L_e(F_P(y)),U_e(F_P(y)))\in\widehat{\mathcal C}_{n,\alpha}(y)\text{ for every }y\in\mathbb R\}\ge1-\alpha\) for every \(n\), including \(n_a=0\), arbitrary atoms, and contact with \(F_P(y)\in\{0,1\}\). The guarantee follows by combining a propensity Hoeffding interval with a conditional Dvoretzky--Kiefer--Wolfowitz band and propagating their joint rectangle through the full piecewise endpoint map.
statements.proof_tex:
Fix a positive integer \(n\) and \(0<\alpha<1\).  Let
\[
 E_e=\{|\widehat e_n-e|\le\delta_e\}.
\]
Apply \(\mathrm{lem:hoeffding\text{-}bounded\text{-}mean}\) to the independent variables \(\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}\in[0,1]\), whose common mean is \(e\) by the definition of the propensity.  Since \(\delta_e^2=\log(4/\alpha)/(2n)\),
\[
 \Pr(E_e^c)
 \le 2\exp(-2n\delta_e^2)
 =2\exp\{-\log(4/\alpha)\}
 =\frac{\alpha}{2}. \tag{1}
\]
Because both \(e\) and \(\widehat e_n\) lie in \([0,1]\), the event \(E_e\) implies \(e\in I_e\), including when the untrimmed Hoeffding interval crosses zero or one.

For \(n_a>0\), define
\[
 E_F=\left\{\sup_{y\in\mathbb R}|\widehat F_{P,n}(y)-F_P(y)|\le\delta_F\right\}.
\]
Under \(\mathrm{ass:iid\text{-}sampling}\), conditional on the treatment indicators and on \(n_a=m>0\), the \(m\) outcomes with \(A_i=a\) are independent and have common distribution function \(F_P\).  Thus \(\mathrm{lem:dkw\text{-}massart\text{-}cdf\text{-}band}\), applied conditionally, gives
\[
 \Pr(E_F^c\mid A_1,\ldots,A_n)
 \le 2\exp(-2m\delta_F^2)
 =\frac{\alpha}{2}
 \qquad\text{on }\{n_a=m>0\}. \tag{2}
\]
Summing (2) over all treatment-indicator configurations yields
\[
 \Pr(n_a>0,E_F^c)\le\frac{\alpha}{2}. \tag{3}
\]
On \(E_F\), clipping the empirical interval to \([0,1]\) cannot remove the true value \(F_P(y)\in[0,1]\), so \(F_P(y)\in I_F(y)\) simultaneously for every \(y\).
Combining (1) and (3) by the union bound,
\[
 \Pr\bigl(E_e\cap(\{n_a=0\}\cup E_F)\bigr)\ge1-\alpha. \tag{4}
\]

On \(E_e\cap E_F\) with \(n_a>0\), one has simultaneously for every \(y\in\mathbb R\)
\[
 e\in I_e,
 \qquad
 F_P(y)\in I_F(y).
\]
Therefore the generating set in \(\mathrm{def:honest\text{-}band}\) contains
\[
 \bigl(L_e(F_P(y)),U_e(F_P(y))\bigr)
\]
for every \(y\), and its coordinatewise rectangular hull contains that pair as well.  On \(\{n_a=0\}\), the same conclusion holds because the definition sets \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_{n,\alpha}(y)=[0,1]^2\).  Equation (4) consequently proves
\[
 \Pr\left\{
 \bigl(L_e(F_P(y)),U_e(F_P(y))\bigr)
 \in\widehat{\mathcal C}_{n,\alpha}(y)
 \text{ for every }y\in\mathbb R
 \right\}\ge1-\alpha.
\]
By \(\mathrm{thm:cdf\text{-}endpoints\text{-}sharp}\), the covered pair is the exact causal CDF endpoint pair.  The Dvoretzky--Kiefer--Wolfowitz inequality is distribution-free and permits atoms.  Moreover, the last containment uses membership of the true point in the generating rectangle rather than continuity of \((\eta,p)\mapsto(L_\eta(p),U_\eta(p))\); hence it remains valid at \(p=0\), \(p=1\), and at every discontinuous face of the piecewise endpoint map.
statements.justification: This gives honest finite-sample simultaneous coverage for the mutual-AC piecewise endpoint pair, including atoms and support contacts.
statements.gap: Existing scalar or sensitivity-index inference does not provide this distribution-free threshold-indexed guarantee.
statements.consumer: The band supplies simultaneous uncertainty for the newly derived mutual-absolute-continuity CDF endpoint map.

statements.statement:
For every integer \(m\ge1\), if \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\) are independent random variables satisfying \(0\le Z_i\le1\) almost surely and \(\mu=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m E[Z_i]\), then for every \(t>0\),
\[
 \Pr\left(\left|m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m Z_i-\mu\right|>t\right)\le2\exp(-2mt^2).
\]

source.verbatim_statement: If X1,...,Xn are independent random variables with ai <= Xi <= bi for all i, then for any epsilon > 0, Pr(|Xbar-E[Xbar]| >= epsilon) <= 2 exp(-2 n^2 epsilon^2 / sum_i (bi-ai)^2).

upstream.citation: Wassily Hoeffding, Probability Inequalities for Sums of Bounded Random Variables, JASA 58(301):13-30 (1963), DOI 10.1080/01621459.1963.10500830
upstream.locator: Theorem 2; two-sided form by applying the one-sided bound to Xi and -Xi and summing the two tails

attestation.note: Exact theorem statement checked in the publicly accessible UC Berkeley repository author copy of Ben-David et al., Machine Learning 79 (2010), Proposition 1, which explicitly identifies it as Hoeffding's inequality; setting ai=0, bi=1 yields the cited node (strict > follows from >=). Primary source is Hoeffding 1963 Theorem 2.

statements.statement:
For every integer \(m\ge1\), if \(X_1,\ldots,X_m\) are independent real random variables with common distribution function \(F\), and \(\widehat F_m\) is their empirical distribution function, then for every \(t>0\),
\[
 \Pr\left(\sup_{y\in\mathbb R}|\widehat F_m(y)-F(y)|>t\right)\le2\exp(-2mt^2).
\]

source.verbatim_statement: Let Fhat_n denote the empirical distribution function for n iid observations with distribution function F. Then Pr(sqrt(n) sup_x |Fhat_n(x)-F(x)| > lambda) <= 2 exp(-2 lambda^2), without restriction on lambda.
